keyPoints: ["Cell cycle = growth, genome replication, then division into two daughter cells; two main phases, interphase and mitotic phase.","G1: cell grows, forms organelles/proteins, prepares for DNA replication.","S: DNA replicated; each chromosome now has two sister chromatids.","G2: forms spindle-fibre proteins, accumulates energy, prepares for mitosis."]
modelAnswer: The cell cycle is the sequence of events in which a newly formed cell grows, replicates its genome, and finally divides into two daughter cells. It has two main phases, interphase and the mitotic phase, and interphase is itself commonly broken into three major stages: G1, S and G2, giving the three major stages usually asked for. G1 (Gap 1): the cell grows in size, increases its number of organelles, and forms the proteins and enzymes needed to prepare for DNA replication. S (Synthesis): the cell replicates its entire genetic material, so each chromosome now consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at a centromere. G2 (Gap 2): the cell prepares for the mitotic phase by forming proteins needed for spindle fibres and accumulating energy (with more mitochondria formed) to complete division. (Sketch: draw a circular diagram with G1, S and G2 as consecutive arcs of interphase, leading into the mitotic (M) phase.)

keyPoints: ["G1 phase: cell growth and preparation","S phase: DNA replication, sister chromatids formed","G2 phase: preparation for mitosis"]
modelAnswer: Interphase is the period of the cell cycle between two consecutive divisions, during which the cell grows and prepares for division. It is divided into three phases. In the G1 (first gap) phase, the cell grows in size, increases its number of organelles, and forms proteins and other substances needed for the next phase. In the S (synthesis) phase, the cell replicates its entire genetic material (DNA), so each chromosome ends up with two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. In the G2 (second gap) phase, the cell prepares itself for the mitotic phase.

modelAnswer: The spindle apparatus forms in prophase from microtubule fibres radiating between the two poles of the dividing cell. Its fibres attach to chromosomes at their centromeres and to the poles themselves, forming a cage around the nucleus as the envelope breaks down. During metaphase the spindle lines every chromosome up at the equator; in anaphase its shortening fibres drag chromatids or homologues poleward; and once segregation ends the spindle disappears as new nuclear envelopes form.

keyPoints: ["Prophase: chromatin condenses into chromosomes","Metaphase: chromosomes align at the equator","Anaphase: chromatids separate to opposite poles","Telophase: nuclear membrane reforms at each pole"]
modelAnswer: Karyokinesis (division of the nucleus) occurs in four phases: Prophase, chromatin fibres coil and condense into chromosomes, each with two chromatids joined at a centromere; Metaphase, chromosomes align at the equator of the spindle with a spindle fibre from each pole attached to each centromere; Anaphase, spindle fibres pull the centromeres apart and the separated chromatids move to opposite poles; Telophase, chromatids uncoil into chromatin, the spindle disintegrates, and a nuclear membrane and nucleoli re-form at each pole.

modelAnswer: Anaphase is the phase of mitosis in which spindle fibres pull on the centromeres, which split so that the two sister chromatids of each chromosome separate from each other. The individual chromatids, now counted as separate chromosomes, are pulled along the spindle fibres until they reach their respective poles of the cell.

keyPoints: ["Both: cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm into two daughter cells, starting during telophase.","Animal cell: cytokinesis by cleavage - membrane pinches inward at the middle.","Plant cell: cytokinesis by forming a new cell wall (cell plate) across the centre, because the rigid wall prevents pinching."]
modelAnswer: Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm that produces two separate daughter cells, and it starts while telophase is still in progress; its pattern differs between animal and plant cells because a plant cell has a rigid cell wall and an animal cell does not. In an animal cell, cytokinesis occurs by cleavage: the cell membrane pinches inward at the middle (forming a cleavage furrow) until it constricts all the way through, splitting the cell into two. In a plant cell, because the rigid cell wall prevents pinching, cytokinesis instead occurs by the formation of a new cell wall (a cell plate) that grows outward from the centre of the cell to the existing wall, dividing the cell into two.

keyPoints: ["Furrow inward versus plate outward","Ground each claim in the quoted textbook line"]
modelAnswer: Animal cytokinesis pinches the membrane inward along a cleavage furrow until one cell becomes two. Plant cytokinesis instead builds a cell plate across the equator from Golgi vesicles, laying down new wall material between the daughters and finishing with two walled cells.

keyPoints: ["Equational division is the shared signature","Ground each claim in the quoted textbook line"]
modelAnswer: Meiosis II mirrors mitosis because both are equational: no pairing or crossing over precedes them, chromosomes line up singly on the equator, and sister chromatids separate to give cells retaining the same chromosome number as the starting cell. The difference lies only in setting, since meiosis II begins with haploid cells produced by meiosis I rather than with a diploid cell.
stem: Meiosis II is identical to mitosis, explain.

modelAnswer: Meiosis is a reduction division: it reduces the chromosome number of a diploid (2n) parent cell to half, producing haploid (n) daughter cells (gametes). When two haploid gametes, one from each parent, fuse at fertilization, the full diploid (2n) chromosome number is restored in the zygote. In this way meiosis prevents the chromosome number from doubling every generation and keeps it constant from one generation to the next.
stem: How does meiosis contribute in maintaining the number of chromosomes?

keyPoints: ["Crossing over (meiosis I): exchanges DNA segments between homologous chromatids, creating new gene combinations.","Independent combination of chromosomes into gametes mixes maternal/paternal chromosomes differently each time.","Together these two events are the source of genetic variation in gametes and zygotes."]
modelAnswer: Meiosis produces new combinations of genes in the gametes, and hence in the zygote formed at fertilisation, through two key events. First, crossing over during meiosis I exchanges segments of DNA between homologous (non-sister) chromatids, producing chromatids with new gene combinations. Second, homologous chromosomes and their combinations are distributed independently into different gametes, so each gamete ends up with a different mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Together, crossing over and this independent chromosome combination are the two important events that give rise to genetic variation among offspring.
stem: How does meiosis contribute to genetic variations?

keyPoints: ["Maintains species-specific chromosome number across generations (haploid gametes fuse back to diploid).","Produces genetic variation via crossing over and independent chromosome combination, aiding survival in a changing environment."]
modelAnswer: Two reasons meiosis is useful: (1) Maintenance of chromosome number - diploid germ cells undergo meiosis to produce haploid gametes, so when two haploid gametes fuse at fertilisation, the resulting zygote has the normal diploid chromosome number for the species (e.g. humans: 23 + 23 = 46 chromosomes), keeping the chromosome number constant across generations. (2) Genetic variation - crossing over and the independent combination of chromosomes during meiosis produce new gene combinations in the gametes, giving offspring genetic variation that helps a species survive in a changing environment.
stem: Give two reasons why meiosis is useful.

keyPoints: ["Mitosis: somatic cells, one division, two diploid daughter cells identical to parent","Meiosis: germ cells, two divisions, four haploid daughter cells with new gene combinations"]
modelAnswer: Mitosis and meiosis differ in several ways. Mitosis occurs in somatic (body) cells, while meiosis occurs in germ line cells. A cell dividing by mitosis divides only once, while a cell undergoing meiosis divides twice. Mitosis produces two daughter cells, while meiosis produces four daughter cells. The daughter cells produced by mitosis are diploid and genetically identical to the parent cell, while all daughter cells produced by meiosis are haploid, with a chromosome number reduced to half that of the parent and a changed genetic makeup due to crossing over. Daughter cells from mitosis become part of the somatic body, while those from meiosis become gametes involved in sexual reproduction.

The cell essentially stalls halfway through meiosis.
